newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Angolan approves UNITA talks with diamond firms.
newsitem.headline: Angolan approves UNITA talks with diamond firms.

text.p: Angola's former rebel movement UNITA, which controls most of the country's diamond areas, has been given government approval to talk to foreign companies about exploiting reserves in its areas, industry and political sources said.

"Endiama (the state diamond company) has told us to talk to the companies and agree on a percentage share of profits. We are already doing this with several of the companies," a senior UNITA official told Reuters this week.

Companies including Brazil's Odebrecht, Russia's Almazi Rossi-Sakha, Australia's Ashton Mining and South Africa's Branch Energy group have been granted mining concessions in the diamond-rich Lunda Norte province, which is 80 percent UNITA-controlled.
De Beers, the world's largest producer, has been granted three licences to prospect for diamonds in both government and UNITA areas.
Endiama has for long tried to make a deal with UNITA on the carving up of proceeds from the diamond areas which produce some of the world's best quality gems.

The government is eager to increase its estimated $200 million a year share of the country's diamond wealth. UNITA, by contrast, rakes in $300 million to $600 million from diamonds in its areas of control.
Talks on the diamonds began in July last year coupled with a a national peace initiative, led by the United Nations, to end the country's 19-year civil war.
UNITA has tightly guarded its diamond areas, mainly based on rivers in the northeast, to fund its guerrilla war.

But since the signing of the Lusaka Protocol to end two decades of civil war, and with implementation of a peace plan now reaching its last stretch, UNITA has been forced to show more flexibility over its diamond share.

It is also set to head the ministry of mines, one of four ministries seconded to it under the Lusaka Protocol, in a unity government with the ruling Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA).

But industry sources said the government's blessing for UNITA to enter talks with foreign companies appeared to be its way of breaking the impasse over diamonds. "This is not a deal on the diamond areas. The government has merely said go ahead and talk to the companies. It will also give the government, through the companies, access to the Cuango River valley," the source said.
The source said UNITA's involvement with foreign companies would help to make Angola's diamond industry more transparent and especially provide a clearer picture of UNITA production.
"We will be able to get a better idea of production on UNITA's side," one industry source said.

UNITA appears to be on the way to formalising its diamond business and has created its own diamond mining company which hopes to enter into joint ventures with foreign mining companies already on the ground, several sources said.
They added that UNITA and foreign companies would discuss what percentage each partner would get from the development of the concessions.
Angola's Endiama would in turn retain diamond revenues already paid to it by the companies.
More mining concessions are to be announced shortly by the council of ministers headed by Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
